replacement: “What is there left to tell? I was lying there, and I thought I heard the master shout. Just before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch had suddenly got up and gone out, and then he let out a scream, and after that it was all silent and dark. I lay there waiting, my heart thumping. I couldn’t stand it. In the end I got up and went out. The window on the left, the one facing the garden, was standing open. I stepped over to the left and listened for whether he was sitting in there alive, and I heard the master moving about and sighing. So I knew he was alive. ‘Ech!’ I thought. I went up to the window and called to him, ‘It’s me.’ And he called back, ‘He’s been here, he’s been here; he’s run off.’ He meant Dmitri Fyodorovitch had been. ‘He’s killed Grigory!’ ‘Where?’ I whispered. ‘There, in the corner,’ he said, and pointed. He was whispering too. ‘Wait a bit,’ I said. I went to the corner of the garden to look, and there was Grigory Vassilyevitch, lying by the wall, covered in blood and out cold. So it’s true, I thought, Dmitri Fyodorovitch really has been here. And on the spot I decided to put an end to it all. Grigory Vassilyevitch, even if he was alive, would never know what happened, lying there senseless like that. The one danger was that Marfa Ignatyevna might wake up. I felt that at the time. But the longing to get it done had come over me so badly that I could scarcely breathe. I went back to the window and told the master, ‘She’s here, she’s come; Agrafena Alexandrovna has come and wants to be let in.’ And he jumped like a baby. ‘Where is she?’ he gasped, but he couldn’t believe it. ‘She’s standing out there,’ I said. ‘Open up.’ He looked out of the window at me, half believing and half suspicious, and afraid to open. ‘Why, he’s afraid of me now,’ I thought. And it struck me as funny. So I thought of knocking on the window frame, right there before his eyes, with those taps we had agreed on as the sign that Grushenka had come. He didn’t seem to trust my word, but the moment he heard the taps, he ran to open the door. He opened it. I would have gone in, but he stood in the doorway so I couldn’t get past. ‘Where is she? Where is she?’ He stared at me, shaking all over. ‘Well,’ I thought, ‘if he’s that frightened of me, it looks bad!’ And my legs went weak with fear that he wouldn’t let me in, or would shout, or that Marfa Ignatyevna would come running, or that something else would go wrong. I can’t remember now, but I must have stood there pale, facing him. I whispered to him, ‘Why, she’s there, right under the window; how can you not see her?’ ‘Bring her, then, bring her.’ ‘She’s scared,’ I said; ‘the noise frightened her, she’s hiding in the bushes; go and call her yourself from the study.’ He ran to the window and put the candle on the sill. ‘Grushenka,’ he cried, ‘Grushenka, are you there?’ He cried it, but he wouldn’t lean out of the window, and he wouldn’t step away from me, because he was in a panic. He was so frightened he didn’t dare turn his back on me. ‘Why, there she is,’ I said. I went up to the window and leaned right out. ‘There she is; she’s in the bush, laughing at you, can’t you see her?’ All at once he believed it. He was shaking all over—he was terribly crazy about her—and he leaned right out of the window. I snatched up the iron paperweight from his table; you remember it, about three pounds in weight? I swung it and struck him on the top of the skull with the corner. He didn’t even cry out. He just sagged down, and I struck him again, and a third time. By the third blow I knew I had broken his skull. He suddenly rolled over on his back, face up, covered in blood. I looked round. There was no blood on me, not a spot. I wiped the paperweight and put it back. Then I went to the ikons, took the money out of the envelope, and dropped the envelope on the floor with the pink ribbon next to it. I went out into the garden, shaking all over, straight to the apple tree with the hollow in it—you know the hollow. I’d marked it long before and left a rag and a scrap of paper ready inside. I wrapped all the notes in the rag and shoved it deep into the hole. And there it stayed for over two weeks. I took it out afterwards, when I came out of the hospital. I went back to my bed and lay down, thinking, ‘If Grigory Vassilyevitch has been killed outright, it may turn out badly for me. But if he’s not killed and he recovers, it’ll be first-rate, because then he’ll swear that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was here, and so Dmitri Fyodorovitch must have killed him and taken the money.’ Then I began to groan, from suspense and impatience, to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as I could. At last she got up and ran to me, but when she saw that Grigory Vassilyevitch wasn’t there, she ran out, and I heard her scream in the garden. That set it all in motion, and it put my mind at rest.”

“Listen ...” said Ivan, who seemed bewildered again and was struggling to catch hold of something. “Listen. There are many questions I wanted to ask you, but I’ve forgotten them ... I keep forgetting, and I get muddled. Yes. Tell me this, at least. Why did you tear open the envelope and leave it lying on the floor? Why didn’t you just carry the envelope off?... When you were telling me, I thought you spoke of it as if it were the right thing to do ... but why, I can’t understand....”
“Mercy on us! Could anybody think all that out in such a desperate hurry? It was all worked out beforehand.”
“Why not, if I sometimes take on fleshly form? I take on fleshly form and I take the consequences. Satan _sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto_.”
